silhouette: gable roof with 42 deg pitch and 25 cm eave overhang, ridge at 3.93 m above the ground plane
brick chimney breaking the ridge line and topped with a stone cap at 4.73 m
door step and threshold standing 16 cm outside the front wall plane
medium: four exposed frame timbers per long wall, 16 cm wide and standing 7 cm proud of the plaster
windows inset 12 cm behind the wall face with a 6 cm frame, cut as real holes through a 22 cm wall
roof tiles laid as overlapping strips, three rows visible per metre of slope

peg heads at the frame joints, 7 cm across, two per timber

principles: Model the silhouette first: a cottage is recognised by roof pitch, chimney and eave line before any surface detail exists.
Wall thickness is what makes a building read as built. An opening cut flush with the wall plane looks like a decal at every distance.
Variation belongs in the parameters, not in the mesh: four cottages from one blueprint with four seeds beat four hand-modelled boxes.
implementation: Call create({ width, depth, storeys, seed, roofPitchDeg }); the returned group is centred on its footprint with y = 0 at the ground plane.
Attach a chimney pot, sign or lean-to through the named sockets rather than by hand-placing world coordinates.
Use the returned colliders for physics; they are axis-aligned box descriptors, not the render meshes.
observable_checks: Run scripts/kit-proof.py and count features in close.png: at least two from each detail-ladder band must be visible in the frame.
Two instances with different seeds differ visibly in tile hue and timber placement while keeping the same silhouette.
The door socket lands on the wall face, not inside it: its z equals half the depth parameter.

known_limits: Authored creative geometry. Nothing here is a measurement of any real building, joinery method or material.
The poly budget is the triangle count observed at default parameters, not a guarantee at every parameter combination; two storeys costs 4980 triangles and a 55 degree pitch 3580.
Tuned against ACESFilmic tone mapping at exposure 1.0 with no post-processing; a different exposure changes how the fine band reads.
Openings are positioned as fractions of the width, so a cottage narrower than 3 m puts its door and windows uncomfortably close together.

T2 is the same geometry with runtime procedural surface and vertex occlusion (see knowledge.surface-tier-defaults); it adds no polygons and ships no files, and it reads at stylized-game quality, not photoreal.

The T3 bake is not seam-free at arm's length: a 16 px margin removes the island bleed that an 8 px margin leaves on timbers and jambs, but the roof strip laps still read as hard black lines and the 0.75 m Cycles AO distance ends in a visible edge under the eaves.
creative_affordances: Any parameter may be pushed outside its stated range; the range is the band that was proved, not a limit.
Swap the palette and the roof material to move the cottage between the listed looks or to an unlisted one.

defaults.rationale: Proportions tuned so a 1.7 m figure reads as door-height at the door socket and the roof still dominates the silhouette at the far proof distance of twenty-seven metres.

T0.note: Bevelled box from the proof log bounds; footprint and ridge height only.

T2.note: Unmapped colours stay flat on purpose: pane #2f3a3f (glass) and opening shadow #3b362f.

T3.note: Baked by scripts/hero-tier.py from this module's own harness export, not remodelled: 3 cm bevel on every arris, smart-project atlas at 2048, base colour multiplied by family noise, Cycles AO at 128 samples folded into the colour map, roughness baked. The three baked maps ship as two JPEG images because the glTF exporter packs occlusion and roughness into one ORM texture. 1,805,736 bytes, inside the 2 MB cap; the same bake at an 8 px margin is 2,120,012 bytes and would breach it. Rebaked in phase 9D with the Blender bake margin raised from 8 px to 16 px. The dark hairlines that ran down the frame timbers, the window jambs and the strip ends in the 8 px bake are UV-island bleed, and a control bake at 8 px against the same pipeline shows them where the 16 px bake does not (evidence/kits/<id>/T3 versus the two crops kept in the phase report). The wider padding also compresses better. What the margin did not fix, and what a viewer should expect at the close distance: the roof strip laps read as strong black lines - they are real geometry that the bake darkens - and the Cycles AO ray distance of 0.75 m leaves a hard-edged band of shade on the walls and timbers under the eaves rather than a gradient. Editing the pipeline moved the cache key, so params_hash is new and the old cache entry no longer answers. Judged against the T2 close-up: contact darkening under the eaves, sills and window reveals is clearly stronger, while the single 2048 atlas (about 450 px/m) is softer than T2's tiled per-material maps, so T2 still resolves individual roof tiles where T3 shows smooth courses. Emissive glazing is flattened by the bake.

silhouette: 3.55 m post-and-head profile: a 2.36 m post over a stepped base, a 44 cm glazed head and a four-sided pyramid cap with a finial
hook arm reaching 44 cm off the post at 2.6 m, breaking the vertical so the lantern reads as ironwork rather than a bollard
0.46 m x 0.67 m footprint including the arm, small enough to sit against a wall or a path edge

two brass collars at 0.62 m and 2.46 m and a diagonal stay under the hook arm at 38 degrees

the 12 cm brass finial and the 26 cm pyramid cap, four-sided and rotated 45 degrees so a corner faces the viewer
three material slots separated by roughness and metalness: iron 0.50/0.30, brass 0.30/0.35, glazing 0.16/0.0

principles: An emissive material is not a light. It makes the glass read as lit from the inside; the illumination of everything around it still has to come from a punctual light placed at the lamp socket.
Emissive strength above 1 is the only reason KHR_materials_emissive_strength is written at all: at or below 1 the exporter keeps everything in emissiveFactor and the extension never appears.
A small prop earns its detail ladder through separation, not through polygon count: cage posts inboard of the glass, collars proud of the post, a cap that overhangs the head.
implementation: Load it through the thin wrapper templates/kits/gltf/iron-lantern.js: `const { group, sockets } = await create({ scale: 1 });`. create returns a Promise because the geometry lives in a file.
Attach the point light at the lamp socket (0, 2.96, 0) rather than at the group origin, or the light will sit at the foot of the post.
Regenerate with: Blender -b --factory-startup --python-exit-code 1 --python templates/kits/blender/export-village-assets.py -- --asset iron-lantern --out templates/kits/gltf/iron-lantern.glb

Exporter keywords, verified present on Blender 5.2.1 LTS (111 operator properties): export_format='GLB', export_apply=True, export_yup=True, export_extras=True, export_lights=False, export_draco_mesh_compression_enable=False, export_animation_mode='ACTIONS', export_force_sampling=True.
export_lights=False is deliberate: KHR_lights_punctual is not written, so the asset never fights the scene's own lighting rig.
observable_checks: Run scripts/kit-proof.py and count features across close.png and detail.png: at least two from each detail-ladder band must be visible. The lantern is 3.55 m tall and 0.46 m wide, so the harness close view crops the cap and finial -- those two silhouette features are counted in mid.png and detail.png instead.
Parse the GLB JSON chunk: extensionsUsed contains KHR_materials_emissive_strength and the LanternGlass material's emissiveStrength is above 1 (examples/early-slice/kits-gltf.test.js asserts this).
KHR_lights_punctual must not appear anywhere in the file, since the asset was exported with export_lights=False.

known_limits: Authored creative geometry and an art-directed emission value. Nothing here measures a real lamp, a real flame or a real luminance.

The mesh is built in bpy from the parameters in export-village-assets.py rather than opened from a .blend, so no binary source is committed and the asset is reproducible from the script; the shape can only be changed by editing Python.
The poly budget is the exported triangle count (1944 triangles) at the authored parameters. There are no LODs, so a lane of forty lanterns is 78k triangles.
136 KB uncompressed, inside the 2 MB validator cap; Draco is off on purpose because the offline proof harness vendors no decoder.
A renderer that ignores KHR_materials_emissive_strength falls back to emissiveFactor alone, so the glass reads about 1.8 times dimmer rather than failing loudly.
Blender 5.2.1 LTS keyword presence was checked with bpy.ops.export_scene.gltf.get_rna_type().properties; no comparison was made against the 4.5 documentation the source record was written from.

T2 has been available for this blueprint since phase 10C: the harness hands a loaded glTF to the same finishKit a module goes through, and the runtime surface is keyed on the GLB baseColor hexes listed in tiers.T2.families. It costs a per-load UV-scale measurement over every triangle and a vertex-AO bake over 3888 vertices (0.66 s on the proof host, 50 ms for the metal family); it can only surface a colour a hex maps, and an authored map baked into the asset would be tier T3.
creative_affordances: The emissive strength is a dial: drop it to 1.0 for a daytime scene and the extension disappears from a re-export entirely.

title.en: Golden hour dusk with a low warm key

records.summary: Set a low warm sun against a cool sky fill so long shadows describe the ground and every vertical picks up a rim.
records.objective: Shadows are several times longer than their casters and run parallel, and the shaded side of each object is cool rather than black.
intent_signals: make it golden hour
the scene looks like flat noon
add a sunset mood
give the buildings long shadows
warm up this exterior
example_prompts: Light a village exterior twenty minutes before sunset.
Give a terrain model long raking shadows that describe its relief.
Warm a street scene without losing detail on the shaded side.
negative_signals: quantitative solar position for a date and latitude
not_for: Interiors lit by controlled fixtures rather than by the sky.
Scenes that must state a real solar elevation for a date and latitude, which needs a sourced solar model.

principles: A low sun is a shape tool. At 6 deg elevation shadows run several times the height of their casters, and those shadows describe the ground plane better than any texture.
The warmth must be paid for with a cool counterpart. A warm key alone reads as an orange filter; a warm key against a blue sky fill reads as time of day.
The sun disc is the brightest thing in frame and everything else is graded relative to it, which is why exposure sits below 1 rather than the key being lowered.
Fog colour belongs to the horizon band, not to the zenith. Matching it makes distance dissolve into the sunset instead of into haze.
implementation: Declare the sun direction once (elevation 6 deg, azimuth 250 deg) and drive the key, the rim and any painted-in shading from that single value.
Set the fill as a HemisphereLight with a cool sky and a warm-dark ground so undersides pick up bounce colour instead of going neutral.
Add the rim as a second weak DirectionalLight roughly opposite the key with castShadow false; it separates silhouettes from the sky without creating a competing shadow set.
Fit the shadow camera to the visible scene extent (20 m here); an oversized extent wastes the 2048 map and produces the stair-stepping usually blamed on bias.
Use normalBias 0.03 to remove shadow acne on curved surfaces before reaching for a larger negative bias, which detaches contact shadows.
Keep exposure at 0.9 and tune the key intensity against it; raising exposure to brighten the shade will clip the sky.
observable_checks: Shadows on a common flat receiver run parallel and are at least three times the caster height, confirming the stated elevation.
A grayscale screenshot still separates lit from shaded planes, confirming the read does not depend on colour alone.
The shaded side of a neutral object samples as cool and non-zero, confirming the sky fill is present.
Turning fog off changes distance separation but leaves foreground exposure unchanged.

creative_affordances: Sky and sun colours can be pushed well past anything a real sunset produces; the requirement is that all shadows still agree with the one declared direction.
The rim can be recoloured to an invented source, a second sun or a city glow, as long as it stays below the key.
known_limits: Every number in this profile was tuned for ACESFilmic tone mapping at exposure 0.9; under a different tone-mapping curve or exposure the intensities and fog density must be re-derived, not copied.
No renderer run for this record; values are authored starting points.

defaults.rationale: Low warm key with a cool sky fill gives the long-shadow, rim-lit read of golden hour; fog matches the horizon band; exposure below 1 keeps the sun disc from clipping while the key at 3.2 still lifts the lit planes well clear of the fill. Kelvin-to-hex conversions here are authored approximations, not colorimetric transforms (2700K~#ffb46b, 3200K~#ffc58f, 4500K~#ffe4c4, 5600K~#fff4e5, 6500K~#ffffff, open shade 8000K~#cfe0ff).

values.time_of_day: 20 min before sunset, sun elevation 6 deg
values.intensity_unit: three-intensity (lux-scaled for Directional/Hemisphere, candela for Point/Spot; tuned with the stated tone_mapping.exposure)
never: shadows that disagree with the declared azimuth

state_contract.model: World rule set stating what keeps islands aloft and how wind volumes affect a glider, plus glider position, velocity, altitude and anchor state. The rules are fictional but fixed and enforced everywhere.
state_contract.authority: The declared rule set is authoritative and applies to every object in the world. An island that floats for a different reason than the rules state is a world inconsistency, not a decoration.
actions: Launch the glider and ride an updraft.

Toggle the wind overlay.

invariants: The stated levitation rule applies to every island, including background ones.

In unanchored free flight the glider loses altitude outside an updraft and gains it inside one. Anchoring, landing and surface collision take precedence over wind, so a moored or landed craft does not sink because it is outside a current.

An anchor can only be attached to a mooring within line reach, and once attached the line never exceeds its declared length; if the tether constraint and a rock collision cannot both be satisfied the scene freezes and reports the conflict rather than letting the craft penetrate the island.
motion_guidance: Drive the glider with bounded acceleration from wind and gravity, and let the pilot pose respond to turns.
Animate cloud layers and streamers at different heights so altitude change is readable without a numeric display.
known_limits: Fictional world rules: nothing here is a physical claim about buoyancy, air density or flight.

records.summary: A full-size scene photographed as if it were a tabletop model: high telephoto camera, a narrow horizontal band of sharp focus, lifted saturation and hard small-scale sun.
records.objective: A single horizontal sharp band covering 18-25% of frame height contains the hero, and blur increases monotonically toward the top and bottom edges of the frame.
intent_signals: Make it look like a tilt-shift miniature
Diorama photo of a city block from above
Fake miniature effect, toy-like scale
Shoot the scene like a tabletop model
example_prompts: A tilt-shift view of a harbour loading yard so it reads as a tabletop model.
Miniature-looking city intersection seen from a high telephoto camera with a narrow band of focus.

principles: The illusion is optical, not geometric: the scene may be full-size and correctly proportioned, and the miniature read comes entirely from focus falloff, camera height and colour lift.

Triangulate three traits shared by fake-miniature photographs — (a) a high, steeply-pitched telephoto viewpoint, (b) a single narrow band of sharpness with symmetric blur ramps, (c) colour and contrast lifted past reality so surfaces look like painted plastic. Those three traits are the recipe; no named photographer, film or artist is required.

Silhouette rule: masses must be blocky and separable from above — roofs, containers, vehicles and tree crowns read as distinct rounded-rectangular tops with 1.5-3 m gaps between them; a scene that overlaps into one continuous roof plane cannot be saved by focus.

Scale cues run the opposite way here: keep real-world dimensions honest (door 2.0 m, bus 12 m, container 6.1 m, lane 3.2 m) so the eye's only evidence for 'model' is the optics — a fake-miniature look built by shrinking objects reads as a broken scene, not a diorama.

Aerial haze is deliberately absent. Depth separation comes from the focus ramp, hard cast shadows and the 1.5-3 m gaps between masses, so this look intentionally opts out of the usual fog requirement and says so.
implementation: Camera: 22° vertical FOV (telephoto), 45 m height, -38° pitch, orbit clamped to 25-55° polar and 40-120 m distance. Wide lenses restore full-size perspective cues and kill the effect.

Depth of field: focus distance 60 m at an f/1.4 equivalent aperture; the fully sharp band spans 20% of frame height (acceptable range 18-25%), and the blur ramps symmetrically to a 12 px circle of confusion at the top and bottom edges at 1080p. Scale the CoC target with output height so a 4K render keeps the same apparent falloff.
Colour grade: lift global saturation +18% and contrast +10% over the physically plausible values; the hero accent (#d94f3d) is allowed 80% saturation while everything non-focal stays at or below 55%.
Sun: DirectionalLight #fff6e2 at 3.4, elevation 58°, azimuth 140°, castShadow true, shadow map 2048 with normalBias 0.03 — high sun and hard, short shadows are how models are lit on a table.

Materials: a moulded-plastic finish — roughness 0.35-0.5 on vehicles with clearcoat 0.15, 0.6-0.8 on ground and roofs, and every edge bevelled at 2-3 mm so it catches a highlight. Suppress detail below 5 cm: seams, small text and micro-scratches break the toy read.
Motion: move vehicles and figures at 0.6-0.8× plausible speed with a hold of 250 ms at stops and a linear ease — smooth realistic easing reads as full-size, slightly mechanical timing reads as model.
observable_checks: Measure the sharp band in the rendered frame: 18-25% of frame height, and the hero sits inside it.
Blur monotonicity: sample circle-of-confusion at 10%, 30%, 50%, 70% and 90% of frame height — it must fall to a minimum inside the band and rise on both sides.
Disable the DOF pass: the frame should immediately read as an ordinary aerial photograph. If it still looks miniature, the geometry has been shrunk instead of the optics changed.
Check the saturation histogram: the non-focal peak sits at or below 55% while at least one accent region exceeds 70%.

known_limits: Values are authored starting points tuned for ACESFilmic tone mapping at renderer.toneMappingExposure 1.0 with three.js physically-based light units; re-tune every intensity under AgX, Neutral or a different exposure.
No renderer run for this record; values are authored starting points.
creative_affordances: The band can be tilted off horizontal by up to 15° to follow a road or quay; keep it a single band, since two focus zones destroy the read.
Night variants work if the practicals stay hard-edged: keep the DOF band, drop the key to 0.4 and let street lamps at 30-60 candela with decay 2 carry the frame.
Subject is free — rail yards, market squares, construction sites, airports — as long as the masses stay separable from above.

defaults.rationale: Every number here serves one perceptual trick: a real camera close to a small object has a shallow depth of field, so simulating that falloff at a 60 m focus distance with an f/1.4-equivalent aperture and a 20%-of-frame-height sharp band convinces the eye the subject is centimetres across. The 22° FOV and 45 m height remove wide-angle perspective divergence that would betray full scale, the +18% saturation and +10% contrast imitate painted model surfaces, and fog is set to none on purpose because aerial haze is a full-size depth cue that directly fights the illusion.

title.en: Feathered wing assembly and authored flight posing

records.summary: Build a wing as a folding support hierarchy with coherent feather fields and distinguish expressive flapping from computed flight.
records.objective: Expose how the wing folds and how its feather layers remain attached while making the source and limits of airborne motion clear.
intent_signals: wing looks like a rigid paddle
model layered flight feathers
separate flap animation from flight simulation
example_prompts: Give a fantasy owl folding wings with coherent feather layers and a clearly authored hover.
Make an inspectable feathered wing without claiming aerodynamic accuracy.

principles: A feather is not simply a thin rectangle: the cited pennaceous structure has a central rachis, branching barbs and interlocking barbules forming a vane. Represent these at the level visible in the intended shot.
Separate support nodes, overlapping feather fields and surface detail. A silhouette can remain stylized while preserving attachment continuity and an intentional folding order.
Distinguish a factual species reconstruction from an invented wing. Feather count, attachment map, skeletal proportions and asymmetry require matched references when labeled anatomical.
Specify whether altitude and translation come from a path controller, keyframes, measured data or an aerodynamic model. A flap cycle alone does not calculate lift, thrust or stability.
implementation: Create a root pivot and serial folding nodes with stored rest transforms and authored angular limits. Name them anatomically only after choosing the species; otherwise use neutral proximal, middle and distal labels.

Place feather roots along authored attachment curves and orient their shafts with a consistent local frame. Give major feathers taper, a central shaft cue and a vane surface; use texture or normals for barbs unless close inspection warrants geometry.
Organize overlapping layers so closing the wing changes the fan spread as well as the support-node angles. Store feather ordering explicitly to avoid random layer swaps during interpolation.

Assign an independent wing-pose parameter and flight-path state. For a decorative hover, disclose authored altitude, heading and flap phase; for computed flight, let the physical model own body acceleration and derive pose without competing transform writers.
Build obstacle clearance from the widest allowed wing pose, including turns and folding transitions. Distinguish a ground wing stretch from takeoff; a perch state needs its own support/contact rule.
Expose folded, half-open and extended inspections plus a slow cycle. Restore feather fan, node angles, body path and animation phase together on reset.
observable_checks: In folded and fully open poses, every major feather remains attached and neighboring layers do not reverse order unexpectedly.
An underside close-up shows whether the wing is deliberately planar or has thickness; backface disappearance is not mistaken for a fold.
Pause the path and the flap separately: each acts only on its declared state, and the interface labels decorative airborne motion honestly.
Sweep the full wing envelope past a nearby obstacle and verify that the narrow folded pose is not used as the flight collider.

known_limits: The feather source establishes microstructure, not a calibrated aerodynamic wing or species-specific skeleton.
Stylized feather vanes and authored flapping do not predict flight capability, sound, feather damage or air loads.
Authored modeling guidance and prospective checks; no runtime artifact has been executed for this record.
creative_affordances: Invent feather palettes, silhouette exaggerations and ornamental wing motifs; a membrane or mechanical wing may replace the feathered archetype with a different stated construction.

claims.statement: Cornell describes a pennaceous feather vane as branching from a central rachis, with neighboring barbules interlocking to create a coherent surface.
claims.scope: Pennaceous feather microstructure; simplified geometry and folding animation remain authored.

title.en: Masonry arch units, springing supports and centering

records.summary: Construct a stone arch from discrete wedge-like units and distinguish temporary erection support from the finished opening.
records.objective: Reveal arch depth, unit joints and supporting interfaces in assembly and cutaway views without pretending that placement alone proves stability.
intent_signals: arch stones look pasted onto a torus
show temporary arch support
explain stone arch assembly
example_prompts: Build an exploded masonry arch with visible wedge units and removable timber centering.
Create a fantasy gateway whose arch has depth and clear support interfaces.

principles: The documented Over Bridge construction used curved timber centring to hold its wedge-shaped stones during erection. This supplies a concrete assembly precedent, not a universal construction sequence or sizing rule.
Treat the opening profile, arch-ring thickness, depth and block joints as independent authored dimensions. A surface texture alone cannot expose how discrete units meet.
Keep temporary centering distinct from permanent piers/abutments and surrounding infill. Do not make one decorative crown block a universal explanation of structural safety.
If stability is explored, declare the contact/gravity model and support restraints explicitly. A visually assembled arch and an equilibrated arch are different outcomes.
implementation: Choose an authored semicircular example with positive inner radius, larger outer radius and finite extrusion depth. Partition its angular extent into adjacent unit intervals and retain shared joint planes, allowing a deliberate mortar gap or contact representation.

Name arch ring, crown unit if present, springing interfaces, side supports, backing/infill and temporary centering. Give the intrados and end faces actual geometry so a view through the opening does not reveal an unintentional hollow shell.

Build centering beneath the intrados as a separate removable assembly with its own footings/support points. In an erection storyboard, keep it visible until the declared completion step; this animation remains explanatory unless mechanics are solved.
Store assembled transforms and explode offsets separately. Material variation can reveal stone units and mortar joints, but random stone rotations should not silently destroy intended joint contact.

For a declared rigid-block experiment, let gravity, unilateral contacts, friction assumptions and restrained supports own block motion. For a diagram, use explanatory arrows instead and do not label them calculated thrust or stress.

Inspect isolated units, the rear face and a transverse slice. Reset returns the same blocks and centering to saved states; removing a unit in a static illustration should not imply a computed collapse response.
observable_checks: Rotate to the back and underside: units have finite depth, shared joint boundaries and a continuous declared arch-ring profile.
The centering lift/removal control affects the temporary assembly only; permanent supports do not disappear with it.
The assembled-state view shows both springing interfaces reaching their supports, without a hidden floating torus behind decorative blocks.
If stability output is enabled, changing restraints or removing a block triggers the stated solver or an explicit unsupported-state message, not a canned success badge.

known_limits: English Heritage source is an Over Bridge construction account; block geometry and sequence here are authored alternatives.
No masonry capacity, compression-only equilibrium, mortar behavior, seismic resistance or safety follows from this visual archetype.
Authored modeling guidance and prospective checks; no runtime artifact has been executed for this record.
creative_affordances: Use round, segmental, pointed or fictional opening profiles with independently authored block layouts; do not force every arch to use a semicircle or prominent keystone.

title.en: Night market street with layered light

records.summary: Build a dense street where the lighting is made of many small owned sources and the crowd flows along readable lanes.
records.objective: Build a night market street I can walk down, with stalls, hanging lamps, steam and a crowd that keeps to lanes.
intent_signals: Build a busy night market street scene I can explore.
Design a night street where the lighting comes from the stalls themselves.
example_prompts: Build a night market street with lit stalls, hanging lamps and pedestrians walking in lanes.
Design a dense market street with legible circulation and stall variety.
negative_signals: Not a crowd dynamics or evacuation simulation.
Not a real place: signage, goods and architecture are invented.
not_for: Not a crowd dynamics or evacuation simulation.
Not a real place: signage, goods and architecture are invented.

entities.name: Stall modules
entities.guidance: Author a small set of stall archetypes with real structure: frame, counter, awning, storage below and goods above, then vary them rather than repeating one prop.

entities.name: Practical lights
entities.guidance: Give every visible light a physical fixture and a declared owner stall, so the light plan and the object plan are the same plan.

entities.name: Crowd lanes
entities.guidance: Define walking lanes with widths and let pedestrians follow them with spacing, so density reads as circulation and not as a scatter.

state_contract.model: Street layout with stall slots, per-stall light fixtures with on and off states, lane graph with capacity, and pedestrian agents with position, speed and a target lane. Trading state per stall is a discrete value.
state_contract.authority: The lane graph and stall slots own the layout; pedestrians follow the lanes and never walk through stalls. Light state belongs to its stall and is not a global switch.
actions: Walk down the street and stop at a stall.
Open or close a stall and see its light and crowd change.
Change the time of evening to shift ambient light while practicals stay on.
Reset crowd positions and stall states.

invariants: Every local artificial light reads as belonging to a visible fixture. Sky and moon ambience and a declared editorial fill remain legitimate art choices; what the rule forbids is an invisible lamp standing in for a stall fixture.
Pedestrians stay inside lane bounds and maintain a minimum spacing rather than overlapping.

A closed stall goes dark, which is this scene authored trading rule rather than a universal property of markets, and its queue follows the declared dispersal or reroute behaviour instead of standing at an unlit counter.
Lane capacity is checked at spawn and at junctions: agents queue or reroute when a lane is full instead of overlapping, and movement is swept so a crowded junction never resolves by interpenetration.
motion_guidance: Give pedestrians bounded acceleration and turn rate so the crowd changes direction believably at junctions.
Animate steam, awning sway and hanging lamp motion at different frequencies, since synchronised motion reads as a single mechanical loop.
known_limits: Signage and goods are invented: avoid reproducing real brands and trademarks. Ordinary writing systems and languages are welcome, and a legible invented business name is usually the better choice than illegible decoration.
Crowd behaviour is authored steering, not a validated pedestrian model.
Authored guidance only: no scene runtime, rendering or numerical calibration has been run for this recipe.

object_craft.structure: Frame, counter, canopy and storage as separate parts with visible joints, plus goods arranged as stacks rather than as a texture.
object_craft.material: Worn timber and painted metal families with fabric awnings; keep material variation between stalls so repetition is not read as cloning.
object_craft.articulation: Awnings and hanging goods sway on a shared wind parameter with per-object phase.

object_craft.structure: Bulb, shade and cable modelled explicitly, with cables sagging between anchor points.
object_craft.material: Warm emissive bulbs with a distinct cooler signage family, so the two light types stay separable.
object_craft.articulation: Lamps swing gently and their light follows the fixture transform.

object_craft.structure: Simple pedestrians with readable silhouettes, carrying bags or food so their purpose is legible.
object_craft.material: Desaturated clothing palette with a few accent characters so the crowd supports rather than competes with the stalls.
object_craft.articulation: Feet are planted from travelled distance; heading follows resolved velocity.

physical_contract.scope: Authored pedestrian steering along lanes with spacing; no physical crowd forces or contact resolution.
colliders: Capsule agents against stall bounds and street furniture.
driving: Bounded acceleration and turn rate toward the next lane waypoint with spacing avoidance.
contact: Agents slide along stall bounds and do not overlap each other beyond the stated spacing.
checks: No agent path crosses a stall footprint.
Closing a stall darkens only its own fixtures.

creative_affordances: The market can be coastal, mountain or fictional; the lighting logic survives any culture-neutral art direction.
Weather is a free choice: light rain adds reflections that make the practical lights work harder.

records.summary: Apply rotations and reflections to labeled square corners and compare operation order.
records.objective: Show the eight symmetries of a labeled square and compare rotate-then-reflect with reflect-then-rotate.
intent_signals: Show the eight symmetries of a labeled square and compare rotate-then-reflect with reflect-then-rotate.
Apply rotations and reflections to labeled square corners and compare operation order.
example_prompts: Show the eight symmetries of a labeled square and compare rotate-then-reflect with reflect-then-rotate.
Create an explorable 3D explanation of square symmetry group with composition table.
negative_signals: The notation D4 here means eight symmetries; some texts use D8 for the same group.
not_for: The notation D4 here means eight symmetries; some texts use D8 for the same group.

entities.name: Labeled square
entities.guidance: Use a thin plate with four distinct corner glyphs and a fixed ghost reference outline; preserve side adjacency.

entities.name: Symmetry axes
entities.guidance: Draw reflection axes and rotation-center arcs separately, with a clear right-to-left or action-order composition convention.

entities.name: Composition table
entities.guidance: Link selected table cells to two operation buttons and the exact resulting permutation; distinguish all 24 corner permutations from the eight square symmetries.

state_contract.model: Corners have fixed canonical labels in cyclic order. Represent each symmetry as a permutation of four vertices; r is a quarter turn and s a chosen axis reflection, with r^4=e, s^2=e and s*r*s=r^-1.
state_contract.authority: Permutation composition owns the resulting corner mapping; animation is a transition between exact group elements and commits once.
actions: Apply a quarter turn or chosen reflection.
Compare both orders of a two-operation sequence.
Inspect all eight group elements.
Undo with inverse or reset to identity.

invariants: Four quarter turns and two applications of the same reflection each restore identity.
Every committed operation preserves square adjacency and pairwise distances.
The selected noncommuting pair yields distinct labeled outcomes in the two orders.
motion_guidance: A planar reflection may be displayed as an out-of-plane flip or an immediate map; label that animation path as presentation, not intermediate planar symmetries.
Lock or queue actions during a transition to avoid double composition.
known_limits: The notation D4 here means eight symmetries; some texts use D8 for the same group.
A 3D cube rotation group is a different subject; this plate has a declared plane and labeled vertices.
Curated recipe only; no runtime scene or rendered behavior has been verified for this record.

claims.statement: The square symmetry group consists of eight vertex permutations preserving the square.
claims.scope: The labels distinguish outcomes but do not change the geometric square symmetry set.

object_craft.structure: Use a thin plate with four distinct corner glyphs and a fixed ghost reference outline; preserve side adjacency.
object_craft.material: Matte plate, corner glyphs with redundant shape/color cues and a transparent ghost reference; avoid backface disappearance during flips.

title.en: Fourier harmonic synthesis with complex phasors

records.summary: Connect a finite bank of odd harmonics to a square-wave approximation and expose truncation near jumps.
records.objective: Change harmonic count and inspect which rotating component contributes to the instantaneous sum.
intent_signals: Change harmonic count and inspect which rotating component contributes to the instantaneous sum.
Connect a finite bank of odd harmonics to a square-wave approximation and expose truncation near jumps.
example_prompts: Build an explorable fourier harmonic synthesis with complex phasors. Change harmonic count and inspect which rotating component contributes to the instantaneous sum.

entities.name: Phasor assembly
entities.guidance: Draw tip-to-tail arrows in an equal-scale real/imaginary plane, one for each retained odd harmonic; arrow k has length4/(pi*(2k+1)). Put frequency and coefficient labels on selectable parts.

entities.name: Complex time trace
entities.guidance: Construct a sampled curve (t, Re S_N(t), Im S_N(t)), with all three axes labeled; the third dimension encodes the second complex component, not decorative depth. Link its imaginary projection to a conventional t-versus-amplitude panel.

entities.name: Target and jump inspection
entities.guidance: Overlay the target sign(sin t) away from integer multiples of pi. Mark jumps with open endpoints and the midpoint value0 as the series convention; do not connect target jumps with sloped interpolation.

state_contract.model: Use dimensionless phase t in[0,2pi] and integer1<=N<=32. S_N(t)=sum(k=0..N-1)4*exp(i*(2k+1)*t)/(pi*(2k+1)); f_N=Im S_N. The square-wave preset fixes these coefficients. Sampling for display uses M>=16*(2N-1) intervals per period plus a doubling comparison; this is an authored resolution rule, not a universal error bound.
state_contract.authority: N, phase, sample count and preset own every arrow and trace. A camera orbit or hidden component does not change its numerical contribution; use a separately labeled mute action to alter the sum.
actions: Select a harmonic and reveal its coefficient, frequency and component trace.
Change N and rebuild the finite sum; retain phase.
Scrub or play phase, pause without phase drift, and zoom around a jump.
Optional coefficient editing enters a labeled custom finite-series mode; square-wave convergence labels are then disabled.
Reset N, phase, sample count and preset.

invariants: Tip-to-tail endpoint equals the independently summed real/imaginary components within a declared floating-point tolerance.
For the square preset f_N(0)=f_N(pi)=0 analytically; at t+pi the imaginary sum changes sign.
Increasing N does not justify a uniform-error-to-zero claim across a discontinuity. Check sampled extrema with doubled resolution before quoting a displayed peak.
motion_guidance: Derive each phasor angle from harmonic number times the same phase; never give it an independent clock.
A cursor projects the complex trace into its imaginary waveform. The connecting segments interpolate displayed samples, not the infinite Fourier series.
known_limits: This is a finite authored synthesis bank, not a measured spectrum, FFT, audio reconstruction guarantee or band-unlimited sampler.
Gibbs overshoot narrows toward a jump as N grows but its limiting relative height does not vanish; avoid claiming every finite N has exactly the asymptotic overshoot.
Authored recipe and prospective checks only; no runtime artifact or rendered result has been observed.

claims.statement: The period-2pi odd square wave has Fourier series (4/pi) sum over positive odd n of sin(nt)/n. Its partial sums exhibit Gibbs overshoot near jumps; increasing the number of terms does not eliminate the limiting overshoot height.
claims.scope: Odd square-wave Fourier series and its jump behavior; not arbitrary sampled-signal reconstruction.

source_refs.locator: 22.6.1 square-wave partial sums and 22.6.2 Gibbs phenomenon, PDF page index 202; Eq.34 at index206

object_craft.family: Fourier harmonic synthesis with complex phasors
object_craft.structure: Keep phasor pivots, vector tips, projection guides and the time-trace frame separately selectable. Rescaling a view must not silently alter coefficient lengths relative to one another.
object_craft.material: Use independent line weights, shapes and labels for mathematical roles. Color and surface finish are presentation choices; do not infer material physics from them.

creative_affordances: A mechanical-looking harmonic bank, clean signal lab or playful ribbon trace can express the same sum; no particular shader or hardware is required.

physical_contract.scope: Derived mathematical geometry and authored inspection; no contact dynamics or calibrated physical artifact.
checks: Tip-to-tail endpoint equals the independently summed real/imaginary components within a declared floating-point tolerance.
For the square preset f_N(0)=f_N(pi)=0 analytically; at t+pi the imaginary sum changes sign.
